newsitem.title: USA: U.S. power transmission data system debuts Friday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. power transmission data system debuts Friday.

text.p: The U.S. electric industry expects a smooth launch Friday of Open Access Same-time Information Systems (OASIS), reaching another milestone in moving the industry toward open competition.
From tomorrow, power suppliers will be able to tap into the system for real-time information on prices and available transmission capacity on the nation's high-voltage lines.
At the same time, they can request to reserve space on the networks to move electricity.

Power providers, using a security code, can access OASIS via the Internet, downloading data on available transmission capacity and fees posted on designated websites as set out by Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rules on deregulation.

Equal access to transmission capacity is seen by regulators and non-utility participants as a key component in deregulating the electricity market because it opens the transmission network traditionally controlled by utilities.
Most market players said they did not expect any big problems linked to OASIS' launch, but would not rule out short-term snags.
"I'm sure there will be some glitches, but we will be okay," said Steve Norris, resources operations manager at Arizona Public Service Co.

"The basic functionalities are there. There'll likely be bugs, but they'll be ironed out," echoed Bill Head, principal engineer overseeing the implementation the data systems in the Mid-Continent Area Power Pool (MAPP).
Norris said he does not expect launch of OASIS to affect transmission prices, but others said the shift to computer orders is likely to raise market volatility in the near term.

"There could be a small bump with all the uncertainty," said one western power marketer. "Within a couple of weeks, people will know where they stand. But until then they won't be so eager to do deals where transmission is involved."
The marketer also said back-up telephone calls will be needed to confirm OASIS orders until confidence in the new system is assured.
"Customers could make transmission requests...(But) there's no on line scheduling with phase one," Head said.
A trader at another western utility said "people are shying away from anything that involves transmission."
He said the separation of transmission from generation prices "allocates tranmission costs to the wholesale market, so I don't see why prices wouldn't go up."
"I don't know what to expect. Initially it would not be a big deal. Nothing is going to change from a physical aspect," said a New York electricity trader.
He said OASIS will provide equal access to market information, but it does not necessarily mean there would be more transmission capacity available.
He said he is wary about the timeliness of the data being posted on the Internet and the ease of accessing it.
"The thing is slower than a dog," he said.
